---
title: "Tools"
description: "Interactive decision-support tools built on published choice experiments and cost models."
---

Three working instruments, not screenshots of instruments. Each carries estimates
from a study and lets you change the assumptions behind them, so you can see how
much of the conclusion depends on which assumption.

They run in the browser. Nothing you enter is sent anywhere.

```{=html}
    <p class="rec-finding">Compare vaccine mandate designs against public preference estimates. Change who a mandate covers, what the exemptions are and what follows from declining, and see which combinations hold public support.</p>
  </div>
```

```{=html}
<li class="rec">

    <p class="rec-finding">Plan the scale-up of field-epidemiology training on a discrete choice experiment and cost model developed for a World Bank business case. Vary intake, duration and delivery mode, and see cost and enrolment move together.</p>
```

## Using and citing them

They are free to use, including in teaching and in policy work. If a tool informs
something you publish, cite the underlying study rather than the tool; each tool
page names it. If you want to adapt one for a different setting, the source is on
[GitHub](https://github.com/DrGenie) and I am happy to help — write to
[mesfin.genie@newcastle.edu.au](mailto:mesfin.genie@newcastle.edu.au).

None of these is clinical advice or a substitute for local appraisal. They are
research instruments that make assumptions visible.
